items.title: Request your employment history from National Insurance records
items.description: Use this form if you need confirmation of your employment history to make a claim for compensation.
items.changeNote: The employment history form has been updated with a new return address.

ai.summary: Use the updated form to request HMRC confirmation of employment history when making a compensation claim for industrial injury, personal injury, medical negligence or other causes.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals filing compensation claims (including employees and self‑employed) who need proof of their employment history
actions: Identify the client’s need for an employment‑history record for a compensation claim
Obtain the latest employment‑history form with the new return address
Complete and submit the form to HMRC on the client’s behalf
Monitor the request and provide the client with the received confirmation

items.title: Find out about the loan charge settlement scheme
items.description: Find out about settling your outstanding disguised remuneration loan charge liability under the loan charge settlement scheme.
items.changeNote: A link to ‘How HMRC will implement the loan charge settlement scheme’ has been added to the section ‘What the settlement scheme includes’.

ai.summary: The loan charge settlement scheme lets individuals or employers with unpaid disguised remuneration liabilities settle their tax, NIC and reduced fees, offering up to £70,000 reduction, a £5,000 extra cut, and exclusion of most penalties, but not late interest or Inheritance Tax beyond a short window.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals and employers who have a disguised remuneration loan charge liability that has not been paid in full, including any related Inheritance Tax liabilities arising from loan‑charge trusts.
actions: Check the client’s loan charge liability letter to confirm they have been identified as eligible for the settlement scheme.
Compare the figures in the settlement offer with the client’s records and discuss any discrepancies with the HMRC caseworker.
If the client cannot pay the full amount, contact the caseworker to arrange an instalment payment plan (up to five years) and explain the interest implications.
Assist the client in completing, signing and returning the acceptance form (by post or scanned email) and advise them to seek independent professional advice if needed.

items.title: Pay tax as a pension scheme administrator
items.description: How to pay charges on payments from registered pension schemes and how long it takes for your payment to reach HMRC.
items.changeNote: Updated guidance to confirm if you use the wrong payment reference number, your payment may be delayed or used to pay a different tax bill that you owe. You can contact HMRC to ask for the payment to be moved.

ai.summary: Pension scheme administrators must submit returns and pay any tax within 45 days of the tax period end, using the correct 14‑character reference. Payments can be made online, by bank transfer, cheque or Government Banking Service, but wrong references or missed deadlines can cause delays, penalties or interest.
ai.whoAffected: Pension scheme administrators of registered pension schemes, including managers of overseas schemes and government departments using the Government Banking Service
actions: Ensure client returns and any tax are filed within 45 calendar days of the tax period end (or by 31 January for reportable events)
Check the 14‑character reference starts with X and matches the HMRC record before paying
Choose a payment method and confirm processing times (e.g., CHAPS/Faster Payments same‑day, Bacs 3 days)
Record the payment reference and date, and monitor for confirmation to avoid penalties

items.title: HMRC videos and webinars for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
items.description: Learn more about Making Tax Digital for Income Tax if you're an agent, sole trader or landlord.
items.changeNote: The recorded webinar link for 'Making Tax Digital if you are a landlord and joint property owner' and the video 'How to sign up your clients to Making Tax Digital for Income Tax' have been updated.

ai.summary: HMRC provides videos, webinars and guidance to help sole traders, landlords and agents prepare for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, including software choice, registration, authorisations and digital record‑keeping, with mandatory use starting from 6 April 2026 for higher‑income earners.
ai.whoAffected: Sole traders, landlords (including joint owners), agents and their self‑employed or property‑income clients, plus any small business with qualifying income
actions: Identify clients whose income exceeds the thresholds and note the applicable start dates
Recommend HMRC‑recognised compatible software that covers all their income streams
Assist clients in registering, authorising the agent services account and signing up for MTD
Set up digital record‑keeping and quarterly update processes

items.title: Starting early is key to less stress around Self Assessment
items.description: Customers encouraged to start their Self Assessment tax return well ahead of the 31 January deadline.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: HMRC urges Self Assessment customers to start their returns early to reduce anxiety, offering online guidance, a checker tool and tips like preparing records, filing in stages, budgeting payments and using digital services. Key deadlines are 31 Oct 2026 for paper and 31 Jan 2027 for online returns.
ai.whoAffected: Self Assessment taxpayers, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses, the self‑employed, PAYE earners, those receiving Winter Fuel or Pension Age Winter Heating Payments, and High Income Child Benefit Charge payers
ai.effectiveDate: Paper return deadline 31 Oct 2026; online return deadline 31 Jan 2027 (2025‑2026 tax year)
actions: Advise clients to gather all records and start the return early, using GOV.UK guidance
Encourage use of the Self Assessment checker tool to confirm filing requirement and register if needed
Recommend filing online before 30 Dec 2026 for PAYE clients and budgeting payments (e.g., monthly instalments)
Highlight digital options such as Making Tax Digital for Income Tax and the HICBC PAYE service for eligible clients
legislationRefs: Making Tax Digital for Income Tax

items.title: Pay General Betting, Pool Betting or Remote Gaming Duty
items.description: How to pay General Betting, Pool Betting or Remote Gaming Duty, and how long it takes for your payment to reach HMRC.
items.changeNote: Updated guidance to confirm if you use the wrong payment reference number, your payment may be delayed or used to pay a different tax bill that you owe. You can contact HMRC to ask for the payment to be moved.

ai.summary: Guide explains when and how to pay General Betting, Pool Betting and Remote Gaming Duty, including deadlines (30 days after each accounting period), required 14‑character reference, payment methods (online, card, bank transfer, cheque) and steps if wrong reference is used.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses that operate remote gambling, general betting or pool betting and are liable for the respective duties, including owners of SMEs and self‑employed gambling operators.
actions: Confirm the client has the correct 14‑character reference number (starts with X) from HMRC online services.
Submit the duty return and ensure payment is made within 30 days of the accounting period end, reaching HMRC by the previous working day if the deadline falls on a weekend or bank holiday.
Choose an appropriate payment method (online bank approval, debit/corporate card, CHAPS/Faster Payments, Bacs or cheque) and follow the timing guidance for each method.
If the wrong reference is used, advise the client to contact Gambling duties enquiries promptly to request the payment be moved.

items.title: Pay Insurance Premium Tax
items.description: How to pay Insurance Premium Tax, and how long it takes for your payment to reach HMRC.
items.changeNote: Updated guidance to confirm if you use the wrong payment reference number, your payment may be delayed or used to pay a different tax bill that you owe. You can contact HMRC to ask for the payment to be moved.

ai.summary: Insurers must file their IPT return by the deadline and pay using the correct 15‑character reference. Payments can be made via Direct Debit, Faster Payments, CHAPS, BACS, online banking, cheque or overseas transfer, observing method‑specific processing times.
ai.whoAffected: Insurers liable for Insurance Premium Tax, including overseas insurers using agents, and any business that has an IPT liability
actions: Verify the 15‑character reference (starting with X) from the registration certificate or notice to file before paying
Choose a payment method that meets the deadline and allow the required processing time (10 days for Direct Debit setup, 3 days for BACS)
If the wrong reference is used, contact Insurance Premium Tax enquiries promptly to have the payment moved
Submit the return even when no tax is due

items.title: How to get authorised to act as a tax agent on behalf of your clients
items.description: Find out the different ways you can get client authorisation including the digital handshake, Online Agent Authorisation service, paper forms and through your client's business tax account.
items.changeNote: The 'Find out the different ways to get client authorisation' section has been updated to remove 'Online Tax Registration Service' as a way to get client authorisation.

ai.summary: After registering as a tax agent you must obtain client authorisation before transacting. Choose the method that matches each tax service—digital handshake, Online Agent Authorisation, business tax account or paper form (e.g., 64‑8). Do not use the client’s HMRC sign‑in details.
ai.whoAffected: Tax agents and their SME, owner‑managed and self‑employed clients who need authorisation to act on tax matters
actions: Register as a tax agent with HMRC
Select the appropriate authorisation method for each tax service (digital handshake, Online Agent Authorisation, client’s business tax account or the relevant paper form)
If the client is digitally excluded, give them the authorisation request link and HMRC contact number
Never use the client’s HMRC sign‑in details; obtain formal authorisation instead

items.title: Check the identity of someone representing HMRC in person
items.description: How to verify the identity of an HMRC officer or an HMRC collector if they contact you in person.
items.changeNote: The process to confirm the identity of an HMRC officer when meeting them in person has been updated.

ai.summary: To verify an in‑person HMRC officer or collector, ask for their ID card, note name and serial number, then call the dedicated verification line to confirm they are genuine; use only for identity checks, not general queries.
ai.whoAffected: SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and the self‑employed who may receive in‑person visits from HMRC officers or collectors
actions: Ask the visitor to show their HMRC identification card and record the name and serial number
Call the appropriate verification number (03000 565 656 for officers, 0300 200 3862 for collectors) and provide the recorded details
Use the verification line only to confirm identity, not for general enquiries
If a collector visits outside 8 am‑6 pm Mon‑Fri, arrange an appointment within those hours before confirming identity

items.title: Compliance checks: prohibition of promotion of certain tax avoidance schemes — CC/FS91
items.description: This factsheet tells you about what happens if you promote certain tax avoidance schemes.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: The factsheet explains the rules against promoting certain tax avoidance schemes, defines promotion and arrangements, outlines civil and criminal penalties, rights during penalty considerations, how to dispute penalties, and where to get help.
ai.whoAffected: Not stated in source
actions: Check that your practice does not promote any prohibited tax avoidance schemes
Familiarise yourself with HMRC’s definitions of “promote” and “arrangements”
Put in place procedures to respond if HMRC considers imposing penalties
Seek HMRC guidance or professional advice if you receive a penalty notice

items.title: Companies House accessibility statements
items.description: These accessibility statements apply to service subdomains run by Companies House.
items.changeNote: Added an English and Welsh language accessibility statement for the Companies House Webchat service.

ai.summary: Companies House provides separate accessibility statements for each of its services, detailing how accessible they are, how to report issues, and the dates the statements were prepared and last tested.
ai.whoAffected: Users of Companies House services, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and the self‑employed
actions: Review the accessibility statement for each Companies House service your clients use
Note the reported accessibility level and any identified issues
Follow the provided procedure to report any problems encountered
Record the statement preparation and last test dates for compliance tracking

items.title: Apply for an increase in tax credits for a backdated disability benefit decision
items.description: Ask for a backdated disability benefit decision to be included in a period when you were claiming Working Tax Credit or Child Tax Credit.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: If a client receives a backdated disability benefit while claiming Working Tax Credit or Child Tax Credit, they can request extra tax credits. Apply within one month using the appropriate HMRC form (adult TC‑DB1 or child TC‑DB2) and follow the submission instructions.
ai.whoAffected: People who have received a backdated disability benefit decision during a period when they were claiming Working Tax Credit or Child Tax Credit
actions: Check the client meets the conditions in helpsheet TC956
Ensure the application is submitted within one month of notification of the backdated benefit
Obtain the correct form (TC‑DB1 for adults or TC‑DB2 for children), complete it in Adobe Reader, save and email it to HMRC
Warn the client that providing false information can lead to a fine up to £3,000 and that HMRC will verify the claim and inform them of any payment

items.title: Approved payers in the middleman scheme
items.description: Check this list of approved payers for non-UK resident entertainers and find out if you need to deduct withholding tax.
items.changeNote: The list of approved payers in the middleman scheme has been updated with one removal.

ai.summary: Payments to non‑UK resident entertainers over the personal allowance require withholding tax unless the payer is on the approved middleman scheme list.
ai.whoAffected: UK businesses and self‑employed individuals who pay non‑UK resident entertainers for appearances or performances in the UK
actions: Determine if the payment exceeds the personal tax allowance
Check the approved payer list to see if the payer is part of the middleman scheme
If the payer is not approved, deduct the required withholding tax
If the payer is approved, no withholding tax is needed and retain evidence of the check

items.title: Authorising an agent to deal with your tax affairs
items.description: Check what a paid agent can do on your behalf. How you authorise the agent depends on the tax, and you may need to use paper form 64-8 or an online service.
items.changeNote: Information about a new online tool to find more guidance about VAT has been added to the VAT section of what an authorised agent can do on your behalf.

ai.summary: The guide explains how to authorise a paid agent for various UK taxes, outlining what agents can do, the forms (64-8, COMP1a) and online methods required, and stresses the taxpayer’s ongoing legal responsibility and need to review submissions.
ai.whoAffected: SMEs, owner‑managed businesses, self‑employed individuals and anyone using a paid accountant or tax adviser to handle their HMRC affairs
actions: Identify the specific tax services the client needs an agent for (e.g., Self Assessment, VAT, Corporation Tax).
Choose the appropriate authorisation method – online service or the 64‑8 form – and complete it with correct agent codes.
Ensure the client reviews and confirms any returns or submissions before the agent files them with HMRC.
Maintain a record of the authorisation and promptly change or remove it when the relationship ends

items.title: Tell HMRC the value of items in your PAYE Settlement Agreement
items.description: Use form PSA1 or send an informal calculation to tell HMRC about the value of items included in your PAYE Settlement Agreement.
items.changeNote: Made it clearer that you need to tell HMRC the value of items in your PAYE Settlement Agreement even if you did not provide any benefits or expenses to employees (a nil return).

ai.summary: Employers or agents must report the value of benefits or expenses in a PAYE Settlement Agreement to HMRC, even if none were provided (a nil return).
ai.whoAffected: Employers, agents and businesses that operate PAYE Settlement Agreements, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed employers.
actions: Gather email, tax year, PAYE reference and applicable tax rates for all employees (including those below the personal allowance).
Submit the values using the online PSA1 form via Government Gateway or email confirmation code.
If preferred, send an informal written calculation to HMRC’s PAYE Settlement Agreements address, noting it may take longer to process.
Ensure all employees who received benefits or expenses are included, even when reporting a nil return.

items.title: Real Time Information internet submissions: 2027 to 2028 technical specifications
items.description: Real Time Information (RTI) Rules and Interface Management (RIM) artefacts and supporting technical specifications for software developers.

ai.whoAffected: Software developers of RTI submission tools and payroll service providers serving SMEs and the self‑employed
actions: Begin testing against the RTI test service from October 2026
Review the technical specifications to ensure compliance
Update payroll software before the March 2027 live launch
Inform clients of upcoming changes and timelines

items.title: Check if a business is registered for money laundering supervision
items.description: Find out if a business has registered with HMRC under the money laundering regulations and report them if they have not.
items.changeNote: The Supervised Business Register has been updated.

ai.summary: The HMRC Supervised Business Register lists companies registered for money‑laundering supervision. Check the register to confirm a counterpart’s registration; if not listed, contact them and, if still unregistered, report to HMRC. Registration provides guidance on AML, terrorist finance and related obligations.
ai.whoAffected: SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed individuals who need to verify a trading partner’s AML registration status
actions: Search the Supervised Business Register for the business’s registration number, name and postcode
If the business is not on the register, contact it directly to confirm its registration status
If it remains unregistered and should be, report the case to HMRC
Advise clients to register for supervision to receive AML guidance and meet their regulatory obligations

items.title: Local reference rents, listed by BRMA and property size (September 2026)
items.description: Local reference rent (LRR) levels by number of rooms and broad rental market areas (BRMA) for residential properties in England in September 2026.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: The publication lists local reference rent (LRR) levels for residential properties in England by room count and Broad Rental Market Area (BRMA) for September 2026, and defines the BRMA and category terms.
ai.whoAffected: Landlords, property owners, letting agents, tenants and anyone dealing with Housing Benefit calculations in England
actions: Check the LRR tables for the relevant BRMA and room category when advising on rent levels
Apply the correct CAT 1A, 1B or 1C definition to each property
Consult the Housing Benefit referral section of the Rent Officer Handbook for detailed LRR calculations
Refer to the National Archives for previous LRR releases if historical comparison is needed

items.title: How to make a voluntary disclosure to HMRC
items.description: Find out about the different ways to make a voluntary disclosure to HMRC if you think you have not paid the correct amount of tax.
items.changeNote:
The address to send disclosures to has been updated in section 'Other potential liabilities you can tell us about in your disclosure’.
The contact address has been changed in section 'If you leave something important out of your disclosure' and in section 'If you’re unhappy with HMRC’s service'.

ai.summary: If you owe tax on income or gains you must tell HMRC about any unpaid tax now. This guide explains how to make a voluntary disclosure, using the updated contact address for submissions.
ai.whoAffected: Anyone who owes tax on income or gains, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and the self‑employed
actions: Identify any client who may owe unpaid tax on income or gains
Advise the client to tell HMRC about the unpaid tax immediately
Send the disclosure to the updated HMRC address as noted in the guide
Ensure the disclosure includes all unpaid tax and any other potential liabilities

items.title: Check if you need to pay tax when you sell cryptoassets
items.description: Find out if you need to pay Capital Gains Tax on gains you make when you sell, exchange or give away cryptoasset tokens (like bitcoin, XRP or ether).
items.changeNote: The video about how cryptoassets are taxed for individuals has been updated.

ai.summary: You may owe Capital Gains Tax when you sell, exchange, spend or give away cryptoasset tokens. Calculate gains per transaction using pooling (except same‑day or within 30 days), deduct allowable costs, report if total gains exceed the CGT allowance, and keep full records.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals—including SME owners, self‑employed and other taxpayers—who dispose of cryptoasset tokens by selling, exchanging, using for purchases or gifting (except to spouse, civil partner or charity).
actions: Identify each cryptoasset disposal and calculate the gain using the pooling rules, noting any same‑day or 30‑day exceptions.
Deduct allowable costs and any capital losses, then total the gains for the tax year.
If total gains exceed the Capital Gains Tax allowance, report the gain on a Self Assessment return or via the CGT real‑time service and pay the tax due.
Maintain detailed records for each token pool: transaction dates, amounts, values in GBP, bank statements and pooled cost calculations.
legislationRefs: Capital Gains Tax real time service

items.title: Check if you have to pay tax on your pension
items.description: Use this tool to calculate how much Income Tax you may need to pay when you get a pension.
items.changeNote: Tool updated to provide an estimate of Income Tax you may need to pay when you get a pension.

ai.summary: The gov.uk tool estimates whether an individual must pay Income Tax on their State or private pension for the current tax year, based on the standard Personal Allowance and other taxable income, excluding foreign income and Blind Person’s Allowance.
ai.whoAffected: Anyone receiving a State Pension or private pension, including self‑employed, SME owners and other individuals with pension income
actions: Collect details of the client’s State and private pension amounts
Gather information on any other taxable income and Marriage Allowance status
Enter the data into the government pension tax tool to get an estimate
Discuss the estimate with the client and advise on any tax planning needed

items.title: Sole traders and landlords earning more than £30,000 urged to act now
items.description: Sole traders and landlords earning over £30,000 urged to get ready for Making Tax Digital.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: From 6 April 2027 sole traders and landlords with turnover over £30,000 must use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, requiring digital records and quarterly updates via compatible software.
ai.whoAffected: Sole traders and landlords whose turnover exceeds £30,000 and who are registered for Self Assessment.
actions: Verify each client’s turnover exceeds £30,000 (gross income before allowances).
Confirm they are registered for Self Assessment and have filed a return in the past two years.
Register them on GOV.UK for MTD for Income Tax and select HMRC‑recognised software.
Set up quarterly digital record‑keeping so updates can be sent on time.

ai.summary: Use form IHT100f to notify HMRC that Inheritance Tax is due and follow the online completion steps.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals or estates that need to report Inheritance Tax due
actions: Download and save form IHT100f to your computer
Open the form using the latest free version of Adobe Reader
Complete the form on‑screen
If the form won’t open, contact online services support

items.title: Check if you meet HMRC's conditions to register as a tax adviser
items.description: Check if you meet the conditions to register with HMRC and interact on behalf of your clients.
items.changeNote: Updates have been made to section 'Who needs to meet the conditions' and 'The registration conditions'.

ai.summary: If you charge for dealing with HMRC on clients' tax affairs, you must register for an agent services account, prove AML supervision, and ensure your business and its relevant individuals meet specific conditions, including no outstanding tax, sanctions, or disqualifications.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses that provide paid tax‑advice services and any officers (relevant individuals) of those businesses, including SMEs, owner‑managed firms and self‑employed advisers.
actions: Check whether your paid tax‑advice activities require registration with HMRC.
Identify relevant individuals – all officers if ≤5, or select at least five officers if >5, based on strategic tax‑advice roles.
Obtain and retain evidence of approved anti‑money‑laundering supervision before applying.
Apply for an agent services account and be prepared to supply additional evidence if HMRC requests it.

items.title: PAYE internet submissions, expenses and benefits — schema 2026 to 2027
items.description: The PAYE internet submissions, expenses and benefits schema and supporting documents for PAYE software developers.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: The PAYE internet submissions, expenses and benefits schema for 2026‑27 is released, with test service support starting October 2026 and the live service commencing in April 2027.
ai.whoAffected: PAYE software developers
actions: Review the new PAYE schema and supporting documents
Begin testing against the PAYE test service from October 2026
Update any PAYE software to meet the new schema before the live service
Inform clients of the April 2027 live service start date

items.title: Ceased or suspended Authorised Corporate Service Providers (ACSPs)
items.description: This list includes details of businesses and sole traders that have had their ACSP status either suspended or ceased (removed).
items.changeNote: Updated ceased or suspended ACSPs list.

ai.summary: The list shows ACSPs whose status is suspended (due to investigations or info requests on AML supervision, filings, or identity verification) or ceased (they quit or breach legal duties). Updates occur bi‑weekly and may lag up to two weeks.
ai.whoAffected: Authorised Corporate Service Providers (businesses and sole traders) and their clients, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and the self‑employed who use their services
actions: Check the published ACSP status list at least every two weeks
Confirm whether your ACSP appears as active, suspended or ceased
If suspended, be ready to provide additional AML, filing or identity‑verification information
If ceased, consider engaging a new compliant ACSP

items.title: List of Authorised Corporate Service Providers (ACSPs)
items.description: This list includes details of businesses and sole traders that have registered as an Authorised Corporate Service Provider (ACSP). This is also known as an authorised agent.
items.changeNote: Updated list of ACSPs.

ai.summary: ACSPs are agents like accountants or solicitors registered with Companies House to act for clients. They must be supervised by a UK AML supervisory body and must not appear on the ceased or suspended list. Companies House does not endorse them; users should research reputation, services, fees and identity‑verification guidance.
ai.whoAffected: SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed individuals who use accountants, solicitors or other agents to file or complete Companies House activities
actions: Check the ACSP is on the current list and not on the ceased or suspended list
Confirm the ACSP is supervised by a UK AML supervisory body
Research the agent’s reputation, services, fees and terms before engaging
Follow Companies House guidance on identity verification when using the ACSP

items.title: Tell HMRC about a gift or other transfers of value in a trust (IHT100a)
items.description: Use this form to tell us that Inheritance Tax is due on a gift or other transfer of value.

ai.summary: Use form IHT100a to notify HMRC that Inheritance Tax is due on a trust, downloading it, opening it with the latest free Adobe Reader, completing it on‑screen and seeking support if it won’t open.
ai.whoAffected: Trustees and agents handling trusts for SME owners or self‑employed clients
actions: Download and save form IHT100a to your computer
Open the form using the latest free version of Adobe Reader
Complete the form on‑screen
If the form does not open, contact online services support

items.title: Apply for an agent services account
items.description: Apply for an agent services account (ASA) to register with HMRC as a tax adviser and use certain HMRC services.

ai.summary: Tax advisers who handle other people’s tax affairs must register for an agent services account (ASA) with HMRC, providing business and personal Gateway IDs, UTR, AML supervision proof, and staff details. Applications are rejected without approved AML supervision.
ai.whoAffected: Tax advisers (including sole traders, partnerships or firms) who deal with HMRC on behalf of clients and receive payment for those services
actions: Confirm you have approved anti‑money laundering supervision before applying
Gather required information: business and personal Government Gateway IDs, firm UTR and postcode, company and VAT numbers if any, AML supervisory body name and proof, and staff contact details
Apply for the agent services account via the Government Gateway, creating sign‑in details if needed and have each staff member create their own Gateway ID
After approval, set up client authorisations, create individual staff IDs, assign appropriate permissions and ensure you do not imply HMRC endorsement

items.title: Insolvency (VAT Notice 700/56)
items.description: Find out how to account for VAT and who to contact if you're an insolvency practitioner and you're appointed over insolvent VAT-registered businesses.

ai.whoAffected: Insolvency practitioners, bankrupt individuals, companies in administration, voluntary arrangements, trust deeds, and any SME or owner‑managed business facing insolvency
actions: Refer clients to the Insolvency practitioner’s handbook sections for notifications, claims, returns and registration cancellation
Ensure dividend payments use the correct 13‑character reference and follow the specified bank details
Advise bankrupt traders to continue filing VAT returns for post‑bankruptcy periods and not include pre‑bankruptcy tax on those returns
Check eligibility for cash‑accounting and apply the post‑insolvency adjustment as required

items.title: HMRC email updates, videos and webinars for Self Assessment
items.description: Learn more about getting started with Self Assessment including registration, tax returns, tax bills and payments.

ai.summary: HMRC provides email updates, webinars and videos covering all aspects of Self Assessment, from registration to filing, payments, and specific sections like self‑employment, property and foreign income. New live webinar links and a crypto‑assets video have been added.
ai.whoAffected: Self‑employed individuals, small business owners and anyone filing a Self Assessment tax return
actions: Advise clients to subscribe to the HMRC help and support email service for updates
Recommend relevant live or recorded webinars based on the client’s situation (e.g., self‑employment, property, foreign income)
Direct clients to specific YouTube videos that explain registration, budgeting, filing and payment processes
Assist clients in setting up budgeting or payment plans using the guidance videos and HMRC app

items.title: Claim a tax refund on your pension by post
items.description: Find out how to claim a tax refund on an additional lump sum or cash payment your private pension.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: If you’ve overpaid tax on a private pension lump sum or cash payment, you can claim a refund by selecting the correct HMRC form, completing it by hand and posting it. HMRC will then repay any due amount via Faster Payments.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals who have received a pension lump sum or cash payment and may have paid too much tax, including those who have stopped work or flexibly accessed their pension
actions: Use the online tool or guidance to identify the correct form (e.g., P50Z, P53, P55) for the client’s pension payment type
Print the identified form
Complete the form by hand with the client’s details and tax information
Post the completed form to the HMRC address shown on the form

items.title: Refunds of UK VAT for non-UK businesses (VAT Notice 723A)
items.description: How to claim a VAT refund in the UK if you're established outside the UK.
items.changeNote: The reference to the 'Northern Ireland Protocol' has been replaced with the 'Windsor Framework'.

ai.summary: The notice sets out how non‑UK businesses that are not VAT‑registered in the UK and have no UK presence can reclaim UK VAT on imports and UK‑based purchases, detailing eligibility, claimable items, minimum amounts, deadlines and electronic or postal submission procedures.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses established outside the UK (including EU businesses) that are not registered, liable or eligible for UK VAT and have no UK place of business or supplies, as well as UK/Isle of Man businesses seeking refunds of VAT incurred abroad.
actions: Confirm the client meets the eligibility criteria (no UK VAT registration, no UK place of business, and their home country offers a similar refund scheme).
Collect the required documents: VAT65A form, certificate of status, original invoices and any supporting evidence.
If using electronic filing, register for HMRC’s Secure Data Exchange Service (SDES) by emailing the Overseas Repayment Unit before 30 November to meet the 31 December claim deadline.
Submit the claim (electronically via SDES or by post) by 31 December of the prescribed year and retain all original documents for HMRC inspection.
legislationRefs: Value Added Tax Regulations 1995 (SI 1995/2518) Parts 20A and XXI
Schedule 9 to the Value Added Tax Act 1994

items.title: Changes to accounting for VAT for Northern Ireland and Great Britain from 1 January 2021
items.description: This guidance gives information about when you can, or need to, account for VAT on your tax return if you're a UK VAT-registered business.
items.changeNote: References to the 'Northern Ireland Protocol' have been removed and replaced with the 'Windsor Framework'.

ai.summary: The Windsor Framework keeps Northern Ireland aligned with EU VAT rules for goods while remaining in the UK VAT system, including services, with HMRC still collecting revenues.
ai.whoAffected: UK VAT‑registered businesses, including SMEs, owner‑managed firms and the self‑employed, that trade goods to, from or within Northern Ireland or provide services involving Northern Ireland
actions: Check client VAT accounting for goods moving to, from or within Northern Ireland follows the EU‑aligned administrative processes
Confirm that services transactions with Northern Ireland are treated as UK VAT transactions
Update client guidance and VAT return templates to reflect the continued UK alignment and HMRC collection role
Notify clients of the change from the Northern Ireland Protocol to the Windsor Framework and its impact on VAT accounting

items.title: Claim VAT refunds in Northern Ireland or the EU, if you’re established in Northern Ireland or in the EU
items.description: Find out how Northern Ireland and EU businesses can claim refunds of VAT incurred on goods in the EU and Northern Ireland using the EU VAT refund system.
items.changeNote: References to 'Northern Ireland Protocol' have been replaced by 'Windsor Framework'.

ai.summary: Northern Ireland and EU businesses can claim VAT refunds on goods through the electronic cross‑border system under the Windsor Framework, provided they’re not established in the refund country and meet the eligibility rules.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses established in Northern Ireland or an EU member state (and their authorised agents) that have incurred VAT on goods in the other jurisdiction and have no fixed establishment, seat of economic activity or place of business in the refund country.
actions: Confirm the client is a taxable person established in NI or an EU state with a valid VAT number and no registration or fixed establishment in the refund country.
Check the claim relates only to goods, meets the minimum claim amounts (€400 for <1 year periods, €50 for full‑year periods) and falls within the 3‑month to 1‑year period limits.
Prepare the electronic claim using all mandatory standard fields and required invoice details, applying the correct expenditure codes.
Submit the completed claim by 30 September of the year following the refund period and keep supporting documentation for any queries.

items.title: VAT on movements of goods between Northern Ireland and the EU
items.description: How to charge and account for VAT on the movement of goods between Northern Ireland and EU member states (VAT Notice 725).
items.changeNote: References to the 'Northern Ireland Protocol' have been removed and replaced with the 'Windsor Framework'.

ai.summary: The notice explains how VAT is charged and accounted for on goods moving between Northern Ireland and EU states under the Windsor Framework, including zero‑rating on dispatch, acquisition VAT by the customer, reporting requirements and special rules for own‑goods transfers and Intrastat.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses that move goods between Northern Ireland and EU member states, including SMEs, owner‑managed firms and self‑employed traders.
ai.effectiveDate: 1 July 2021 (distance‑selling changes) and 1 January 2023 (VAT interest changes)
actions: Determine if the client supplies goods to VAT‑registered customers in the EU and apply the zero‑rate on dispatch from NI
Ensure the EU customer accounts for acquisition VAT on their return
Include the supplies on the client’s VAT return, EC Sales List and Intrastat filings using the correct tax point
If the client’s EU trade exceeds the Intrastat threshold, complete Supplementary Declarations
legislationRefs: Value Added Tax Act 1994, Schedules 9ZA and 9ZD

items.title: Check how to report and pay VAT on distance sales of goods from Northern Ireland to the EU
items.description: How to report and pay VAT due on the distance sales of goods from Northern Ireland to consumers in the EU using the One Stop Shop (OSS) Union scheme.
items.changeNote: The reference to the 'Northern Ireland Protocol' has been replaced with the 'Windsor Framework'.

ai.summary: Northern Irish businesses selling goods to EU consumers that exceed the distance‑selling threshold must account for VAT in the consumer’s country, but can use the OSS Union scheme to file a single return. Those below the UK VAT threshold must first register for UK VAT to join OSS.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses in Northern Ireland (including SMEs, owner‑managed firms and self‑employed) that sell goods to EU consumers, whether above or below the UK VAT registration threshold.
actions: Check eligibility: sales to EU consumers above the distance‑selling threshold and under the Windsor Framework
If turnover is below the UK VAT threshold, register for UK VAT and select activity code 63990 when registering
Register for the OSS Union scheme and complete the OSS return
Keep all required records for 10 years and submit OSS returns and payments as required
legislationRefs: 63990 Distance sales of goods (below UK VAT threshold)

items.title: Inheritance Tax: claim for relief — loss on sale of land (IHT38)
items.description: Use form IHT38 to claim relief on Inheritance Tax if you sell land or buildings from the deceased’s estate at a loss.
items.changeNote: Details on when to use the form IHT38 have been updated.

ai.summary: Use form IHT38 to claim Inheritance Tax relief when land or buildings from a deceased’s estate are sold at a loss, provided the sale occurs within the permitted period (usually 3 years, up to 4 years in some cases) and the claim is made by the person liable for the tax.
ai.whoAffected: The person liable for the Inheritance Tax on the property (e.g., executor or administrator of the deceased’s estate)
actions: Identify any qualifying loss sale of land or buildings within the permitted period after death
Confirm who is liable for the Inheritance Tax on the property
Complete form IHT38 with the required details
Submit the IHT38 claim to HMRC within the applicable time limit

items.title: Tell HMRC about assets previously held in an ‘18 to 25’ trust (IHT100h)
items.description: Report Inheritance Tax due on assets that have stopped being held in an ‘18 to 25’ trust using form IHT100h.
items.changeNote: The 'Declaration' section of 'How to fill in form IHT100h' has been updated.

ai.summary: Use form IHT100h to report Inheritance Tax due on an ‘18 to 25’ trust, downloading it, opening with Adobe Reader, completing on‑screen, and seeking support if it won’t open.
ai.whoAffected: Anyone who needs to report Inheritance Tax due on an ‘18 to 25’ trust
actions: Download and save form IHT100h
Open the form with the latest free version of Adobe Reader
Complete the form on‑screen
If the form won’t open, contact online services support or read the accessibility statement

items.title: Check the recognised overseas pension schemes notification list
items.description: Find schemes that have told HMRC they meet the conditions to be a recognised overseas pension scheme (ROPS).

ai.summary: The HMRC list of recognised overseas pension schemes (ROPS) is published on the 1st and 15th of each month (or the next working day). Inclusion does not guarantee tax‑free transfers; advisers must confirm any UK tax liability before recommending a transfer.
ai.whoAffected: SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed individuals considering transferring UK pension savings to an overseas scheme
ai.effectiveDate: Published on the 1st and 15th day of each month (or the next working day if the date falls on a weekend or UK public holiday)
actions: Check the latest ROPS list on each publication date before advising any overseas pension transfer
Confirm with the client that HMRC does not guarantee tax‑free status and assess any UK tax charge that may arise
Advise the client to obtain suitable professional advice from a regulated financial adviser
Monitor the list for short‑notice removals or updates and inform clients promptly

items.title: Tell HMRC about the end of a qualifying interest in possession because someone has died (IHT100b (death))
items.description: Use this form to tell us that a beneficiary's qualifying interest in possession in a trust has come to an end due to their death and Inheritance Tax is due.
items.changeNote: The declaration section wording has been updated to remove page specific references and clarify the statements that agents and trustees must provide.

ai.summary: Use form IHT100b (death) to notify HMRC that Inheritance Tax is due when a beneficiary’s qualifying interest in possession ends because of death, by downloading, opening in Adobe Reader and completing it on‑screen.
ai.whoAffected: Beneficiaries whose qualifying interest in possession in a trust ends on death and the trustees/agents responsible for the trust
actions: Download form IHT100b (death) and save it to your computer
Open the saved form using the latest free version of Adobe Reader
Complete the form on‑screen
If the form will not open, contact online services support for assistance

items.title: How model assisted valuation delivers large-scale property valuations
items.description: How the Valuation Office Agency uses model assisted valuation and mass appraisal to support large-scale valuation.
items.changeNote: Added PDF 'A Gaussian Markov Random Field model for the valuation of domestic properties in Wales, UK, using INLA'.

ai.summary: The Valuation Office Agency uses a model‑assisted valuation (AVM) and mass appraisal to value 1.5 million Welsh domestic properties for a 2028 Council Tax revaluation, with valuers checking data, targeting band margins and allowing customers to challenge their band.
ai.whoAffected: Property owners in Wales subject to Council Tax, including SMEs and self‑employed individuals with domestic property holdings.
actions: Explain to clients that the VOA’s AVM determines Council Tax bands and that they have a legal right to challenge a band if they disagree
Advise clients to keep accurate property data and records in case valuers sample their property for review
Monitor VOA publications for model specifications, technical papers and external assessment reports to stay informed
Assist clients in preparing evidence and submitting challenges if their property is flagged at band margins or shows unusual valuation changes

items.title: Pay your Economic Crime Levy
items.description: How to pay the Economic Crime Levy, and how long it takes for your payment to reach HMRC.
items.changeNote: Information about the bands for financial years from 1 April 2026 have been added.

ai.summary: The Economic Crime Levy must be paid by 30 Sept each year; rates depend on UK revenue bands, with small entities exempt and larger entities paying fixed amounts. Returns need a 14‑character reference, and payments can be made online, by Direct Debit, card or bank transfer, ensuring funds arrive before the deadline.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses with UK revenue over £10.2 million (band A, B, C, D) that are liable for the Economic Crime Levy, as well as any entity that must submit a levy return.
actions: Determine the client’s revenue band for the financial year and calculate the levy due
Obtain the 14‑character Economic Crime Levy return number and submit the return before the deadline
Arrange payment (online, Direct Debit, card or bank transfer) so it reaches HMRC by 30 Sept, accounting for bank processing times
Check for any partial‑year reductions or over‑payments and advise on refunds where applicable

items.title: Submit a return for the Economic Crime Levy
items.description: Find out how to submit a return and how to amend a return for the Economic Crime Levy.
items.changeNote: The example for who must submit a return has been updated from 'medium-sized entity' to 'band A entity'.

ai.summary: Registered businesses must file an Economic Crime Levy return each year by 30 September, even if they fall below the levy threshold, providing UK revenue, AML activity duration and the return preparer’s details, using the online service and keeping records for possible amendments or penalties.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses that have registered for the Economic Crime Levy, including band A entities and any entity meeting the levy threshold
actions: Confirm the client is registered for the Economic Crime Levy and has a sign‑in for each entity
Collect the client’s UK revenue, AML activity period and preparer’s name, role and contact details for the accounting period
Submit the return online by 30 September and note the 14‑digit return number for payment
If needed, advise the client how to amend the return via their account and handle any refunds or penalties

Contact the software supplier for technical support if you are a developer

Use the software to file the Company Tax Return online

items.title: Negligible value claims and agreements
items.description: How to make a negligible value claim for unquoted shares, and how to check if shares previously quoted on the London Stock Exchange now have negligible value.
items.changeNote: HMRC's list of shares which have been declared as being worth negligible value is now valid up to and including 31 August 2026.

ai.summary: Negligible value claims let owners of assets that have fallen to almost no value realise a loss against CGT. Claims can be made by writing to the tax office or via Self Assessment. HMRC’s list shows previously LSE‑quoted shares deemed negligible up to 31 Aug 2026; unquoted or AIM companies aren’t listed.
ai.whoAffected: Owners of unquoted shares that have become worthless, shareholders of companies previously quoted on the London Stock Exchange, and directors of companies in liquidation or receivership – including SMEs and owner‑managed businesses with such shareholdings.
actions: Check the HMRC Negligible Value Agreement list to see if the share is listed as negligible
Gather evidence – statement of affairs, liquidator/receiver letter, balance‑sheet showing debts exceed assets, and proof no rescue is likely
Submit a claim by writing to your tax office or entering the negligible value on your Self Assessment return
If the company is in liquidation or receivership, include all required documents listed in the guidance

items.title: Provide or update your partnership details for VAT
items.description: Use form VAT2 to tell HMRC about a new partnership or update partner details.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: Form VAT2 is used by partnerships to provide or update partner details when registering for VAT, adding/removing partners, or changing the partnership’s bank account. Up to 8 partners per form; extra forms needed for more.
ai.whoAffected: Partnerships registering for VAT and existing VAT‑registered partnerships that need to add, remove or update partner information, including bank‑account changes
actions: Gather the partnership’s VAT registration number, business name, each partner’s date of birth, National Insurance number and signatures
Print the VAT2 form and complete the registration number, business name and reason for sending
Have each partner fill in and sign their allocated section (up to 8 per form; use additional forms if more partners)
Upload the completed form via the VAT registration portal or post it to the VAT registration applications and changes team; request an accessible format if required

items.title: Residence and foreign income and gains (FIG) regime etc (Self Assessment SA109)
items.description: Use supplementary pages SA109 to record your residence and domicile status on your SA100 Tax Return.
items.changeNote: The notes for the 2025 to 2026 tax year have been updated. References to a source-by-source basis have been removed from the notes of boxes 28 and 29 on page 9.

ai.summary: SA109 pages must be filed with the SA100 to record residence/domicile status and claim personal allowances for non‑UK residents. Use related helpsheets (HS264, HS300, HS302, HS303, HS304) for remittance basis, non‑resident income, dual residency and tax relief.
ai.whoAffected: Non‑UK resident individuals, including self‑employed people and owners of SMEs, who need to submit a UK Self Assessment return
actions: Determine the taxpayer’s residence and domicile status
Complete the SA109 supplementary pages and attach them to the SA100 return
Claim any personal allowances available to non‑UK residents on the SA109
Refer to the appropriate helpsheets (HS264, HS300, HS302, HS303, HS304) for specific issues such as remittance basis or dual residency

items.title: How to get an agent reference number for PAYE
items.description: Find out how to get an agent reference number for PAYE, Construction Industry Scheme (CIS) or Employment Related Securities (ERS), if you are a PAYE agent or payroll bureau.

ai.whoAffected: PAYE agents, payroll bureaus and anyone needing to register as a tax adviser to use HMRC agent services
actions: Check whether you need to register as a tax adviser
If required, apply for an agent services account
Apply online for an agent reference number (provide full name, trading name, phone and email)
Sign into HMRC online services and enrol the PAYE, CIS and/or ERS services

Contact Companies House at xml@companieshouse.gov.uk for clarification

items.title: Using software to file your company's information
items.description: How to send information to Companies House using commercial software.

ai.whoAffected: All UK companies that file annual accounts, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed directors, whether they file directly or use an accountant
actions: Check each client’s current software can produce iXBRL and ZIP files for filing
Advise clients to obtain a company authentication code, presenter account and, if needed, a Companies House credit account
Recommend suitable commercial software and plan migration before the 1 April 2028 deadline
Confirm that any appointed accountants are ready to file using the new software requirements

items.title: Change the details of a UK establishment of an overseas company (OS CH01)
items.description: Use this form OS CH01 to change the details of a UK establishment of an overseas company.

ai.summary: Use form OS CH01 to notify Companies House of any changes to a UK establishment of an overseas company, ensuring the UK establishment address is provided and nationalities/countries are selected from the approved list.
ai.whoAffected: UK establishment of an overseas company (overseas companies operating in the UK)
actions: Confirm the client’s UK establishment address is the physical location where business is carried out
Complete OS CH01, entering the address exactly as the UK establishment address
Select nationalities and countries only from the official standard list provided
Submit the completed OS CH01 form to Companies House

items.title: Company authentication codes for online filing
items.description: How to request and manage the company authentication code you'll need to file information online at Companies House.
items.changeNote: Overseas companies can now request an authentication code using the Find and update company information service.

ai.summary: A 6‑digit alphanumeric company authentication code authorises online filings. Request via Companies House WebFiling (UK) or Find and update service (overseas); it’s sent by post, not email or phone. Keep it secure, change if compromised, and inform anyone filing for the company of any changes.
ai.whoAffected: All UK‑registered companies, overseas companies with a UK establishment, their directors, accountants and anyone filing online on their behalf.
actions: Advise clients to request their code early via WebFiling or Find and update service and allow up to 10 working days for delivery.
Ensure clients store the code securely and treat it like a bank PIN.
Prompt clients to inform you of any code changes and update your records accordingly.
Warn overseas clients they must use Find and update service and can only file package accounts.

items.title: Overseas companies in the UK: registration and filing
items.description: Registration and filing obligations of an overseas company that opens an establishment in the UK.
items.changeNote: Overseas companies can now file iXBRL package accounts online.

ai.summary: The guide outlines how overseas companies (including those from the EEA) must register a UK establishment, the documents to file with Companies House, and ongoing accounting, naming and trading disclosure duties, now using online iXBRL filing.
ai.whoAffected: Overseas companies opening or already operating a UK establishment, including those from the EEA, and advisers to such companies
actions: Confirm the client is an overseas (or EEA) company planning a UK establishment
Register the establishment with Companies House and submit the required documents
Prepare iXBRL package accounts and file them online, complying with accounting, name and trading disclosure rules
Maintain ongoing filing and disclosure obligations after registration

items.title: Filing your Companies House accounts
items.description: How to prepare and file annual accounts with Companies House for your UK registered company.
items.changeNote: Overseas companies can now file iXBRL package accounts online.

ai.summary: All UK‑registered companies, even dormant ones, must file annual accounts with Companies House. The online filing service ended 31 Mar 2026, so future filings require commercial software. Certain iXBRL package accounts, including overseas company accounts, can now be filed online.
ai.whoAffected: All UK‑registered companies, including dormant, micro, small, medium, audited, unaudited, group and overseas companies that need to file annual accounts
actions: Obtain the company authentication code for each client
Use commercial accounting software to prepare and file accounts, as the online service closed on 31 Mar 2026
Check if the client qualifies for iXBRL package filing (e.g., overseas company, CIC, group accounts) and use the required ZIP/iXBRL format
File accounts before the statutory deadline to avoid penalties

items.title: Companies House fees
items.description: A list of all the fees Companies House charges, and how we determine these fees.
items.changeNote: Added the £50 fee for filing overseas company package accounts online.

ai.summary: Companies House fees are set by specific statutory fee regulations and cost‑recovery principles, with a 3.5% cost of capital and no cross‑subsidy. Some documents under the Companies Act 1985 or NI Order 1986 are free, and fees may change as announced.
ai.whoAffected: All companies, overseas companies, LLPs, limited partnerships and other entities filing documents with Companies House, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and the self‑employed
actions: Check if client filings fall under the Companies Act 1985 or the Companies (Northern Ireland) Order 1986 to qualify for free filing
Identify the applicable statutory fee regulations for each filing type and advise on the correct fee
Explain to clients that fees reflect full cost recovery, including a 3.5% cost of capital, and that no cross‑subsidy occurs
Monitor Companies House guidance for any announced fee changes and update client advice accordingly
