items.title: Pay Stamp Duty Land Tax
items.description: How to pay Stamp Duty Land Tax, and how long it takes for your payment to reach HMRC.
items.changeNote: Updated guidance to confirm if you use the wrong payment reference number, your payment may be delayed or used to pay a different tax bill that you owe. You can contact HMRC to ask for the payment to be moved.

ai.summary: SDLT must be paid within 14 days of the effective transaction date using the 11‑character reference. Choose an online, bank transfer or cheque method and ensure the reference matches to avoid delays or misallocation. Wrong references can be corrected by contacting SDLT enquiries.
ai.whoAffected: Property purchasers (including SMEs and owner‑managed businesses) and their advisers who need to pay Stamp Duty Land Tax in England, Wales or Northern Ireland
actions: Obtain the 11‑character unique transaction reference from the SDLT5 certificate or paper return
Submit the SDLT return and arrange payment within 14 days of the effective date, using a method that meets the deadline
Check that the reference entered matches exactly to avoid delays or misallocation; if incorrect, contact SDLT enquiries to move the payment
Advise clients on payment method timings (online instant, CHAPS/Faster same‑day, Bacs up to 3 days) and ensure funds arrive before the deadline

items.title: Seven linked companies shut down after Insolvency Service investigation with Companies House
items.description: The companies appeared unrelated until a joint investigation uncovered similar conduct concerns.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: Seven companies were wound up after the Insolvency Service and Companies House uncovered false filings, misleading audit information and non‑existent offices, highlighting the risk of fraudulent registrations and the need for accurate company records.
ai.whoAffected: Company directors, SME owners and anyone relying on Companies House information
actions: Check client filings for accuracy and completeness
Confirm that registered office addresses are genuine and occupied
Verify audit engagements and retain audit documentation
Direct directors to the Insolvency Service’s Director Information Hub for guidance

items.title: Almost 3 million young adults are ‘quids in’ after claiming Child Trust Fund
items.description: Young people urged to go online to find their Child Trust Fund.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: Nearly 3 million matured Child Trust Funds have been claimed or moved to ISAs, but about 827,000 remain unclaimed, averaging £2,310 each. Young adults can locate their accounts for free via the GOV.UK tool using their NI number and DOB, then choose to withdraw, keep, or transfer the money.
ai.whoAffected: Young adults aged 18‑24 with matured Child Trust Funds, and their parents or guardians
actions: Guide clients to use the GOV.UK Child Trust Fund locator tool with their NI number and date of birth
Advise clients on the three options: withdraw, keep the fund, or transfer to an ISA
Help clients gather required details (NI number, DOB) and submit the request, noting the ~3‑week response time
Inform clients of the average value and encourage timely claim to avoid funds remaining unclaimed

items.title: Claim personal allowances and tax refunds if you live abroad (R43)
items.description: How to claim a refund on tax and personal allowances on UK income if you're not resident in the UK on form R43.
items.changeNote: The personal allowances and tax repayments (R43) form and guidance notes have been updated to reflect the changes to the Double Taxation Agreement between the UK and Israel by the 2019 Protocol which entered into force on 28 October 2019.

ai.summary: Non‑resident individuals can claim UK personal allowances and tax refunds for UK income from the current year and the previous four years using form R43, unless they already file a Self Assessment or have rental income over £2,500.
ai.whoAffected: UK non‑resident individuals who receive UK income such as property rent, pensions, dividends, interest or state benefits and are not already filing a Self Assessment.
actions: Verify the client’s residency status and days spent in the UK
Determine if a tax certificate is required and obtain it
Gather details of all UK income for the relevant tax year(s)
Submit form R43 online or download the PDF and post it, unless rental income exceeds £2,500 – then advise filing a Self Assessment

items.title: How to prove your identity for Companies House at the Post Office
items.description: How to complete your identity verification in person at a Post Office, once you've entered your photo ID details online.
items.changeNote: Added 'Deadline' guidance. You have 21 days from the date you booked the Post Office appointment to complete the verification process and view your result.

ai.summary: Clients must enter photo ID details online, download a customer letter, visit a Post Office with the letter and original ID within 21 days, have their QR code scanned and photo taken, then await the result email to obtain their Companies House personal code.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals needing to verify their identity for Companies House (e.g., directors, company officers)
actions: Advise the client to enter their photo‑ID details via the Companies House online service and book a Post Office appointment.
Tell the client to download the customer letter and keep their original photo ID ready for the visit.
Ensure the client attends any eligible Post Office within 21 days, where staff will scan the QR code and capture their photo and ID.
Follow up to confirm the client receives the GOV.UK One Login email with their personal code or advise next steps if the check fails.

items.title: Submit an enquiry to HM Treasury
items.description: Use this form to send an enquiry to HM Treasury.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: The guidance explains how to submit enquiries to HM Treasury, what content is prohibited, and advises not to use the form for FOI requests or HMRC complaints. It also warns of fraud and provides links to related tax and pension information.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses, self‑employed individuals and other organisations wishing to contact HM Treasury for policy‑related queries.
actions: Check that the enquiry relates directly to HM Treasury before using the form
Ensure the message contains no offensive language, sales content, illegible text or repeated queries
Do not use the form for Freedom of Information requests or HMRC complaints; use the appropriate channels instead
Be vigilant for fraud – HM Treasury will never ask for money or personal details via email

items.title: Trader Support Service users urged to prepare for new platform
items.description: Businesses should prepare now before switchover to continue trading.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: The free Trader Support Service will move to a new digital platform next month; all goods movements between Great Britain and Northern Ireland must be submitted on it from 20 October. Businesses must pre‑enrol after receiving an invitation email (from 1 October) and update their details to avoid disruption.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses registered for the Trader Support Service that move goods between Great Britain and Northern Ireland
actions: Watch for the HMRC invitation email (starting 1 October) and pre‑enrol on the new TSS platform before 20 October
Use the test environment to become familiar with the new system and create a new password
Check and update business details and permissions on the new platform
Ensure the updated profile is saved so declarations can be submitted after 20 October

items.title: Producing Dovey Native Botanical Gin
items.description: Find out how to apply to the Spirit Drinks Verification Scheme, pay fees and comply with the product specification for Dovey Native Botanical Gin.
items.changeNote: Information about the transitional arrangements for existing producers of Dovey Native Botanical Gin has been removed as the arrangement ended on 1 September 2026.

ai.summary: New producers must apply to the Spirit Drinks Verification Scheme, pay fees, undergo verification visits every two years and stay compliant to market Dovey Native Botanical Gin legally.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses and individuals planning to produce and market Dovey Native Botanical Gin, including SMEs, owner‑managed firms and self‑employed producers
actions: Apply to the Spirit Drinks Verification Scheme before starting production
Pay the registration and verification fees when invoiced
Prepare documentation, equipment and procedures for the verification visit
If non‑compliant, implement changes within the agreed timeframe and inform customers if verification is withdrawn

items.title: National Minimum Wage information for employers
items.description: Find out about the checks we carry out to make sure you're paying your workers at least the National Minimum Wage.
items.changeNote: In 'About National Living Wage and the National Minimum Wage checks — NMW FS1', references to the Department for Business and Trade (DBT) have been updated to the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST).’

ai.summary: The factsheet outlines HMRC’s checks to ensure employers pay at least the National Minimum or Living Wage, how to self‑review payroll records, details on arrears, penalties and tribunal video witness procedures.
ai.whoAffected: Employers who pay workers the National Minimum Wage or National Living Wage, including SMEs and owner‑managed businesses
actions: Conduct a self‑review of payroll records against NMW/NLW rates
Verify all workers receive at least the applicable minimum wage
Identify and address any NMW arrears to avoid penalties
Prepare for possible tribunal hearings, including video witness arrangements

items.title: Pay Stamp Duty Reserve Tax
items.description: How to pay your Stamp Duty Reserve Tax, and how long it takes for your payment to reach HMRC.
items.changeNote: Updated guidance to confirm if you use the wrong payment reference number, your payment may be delayed or used to pay a different tax bill that you owe. You can contact HMRC to ask for the payment to be moved.

ai.summary: SDRT is due on paperless share purchases. CREST trades are auto‑deducted; off‑market trades need a written notice with buyer/seller details, securities info, payment reference and must be paid within 14 days or by the 7th of the following month. Use correct reference and HMRC bank details.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses and individuals who buy or sell shares, especially those making off‑market share transactions
actions: Send a written notice for off‑market share trades including buyer/seller details, securities transferred, reliefs claimed, payment details and a reference number you choose
Ensure the notice and payment reach HMRC within the applicable deadline – 14 days for CREST‑eligible trades or the 7th of the month after the agreement for non‑CREST trades
Use the correct reference number; if an error occurs, contact SDRT enquiries to have the payment moved to the right tax bill
Pay electronically using the UK or overseas HMRC account details provided and allow the appropriate processing time (same/next day for CHAPS/Faster Payments, 3 working days for Bacs)

items.title: CWG2: further guide to PAYE and National Insurance contributions
items.description: Find out about detailed Pay As You Earn (PAYE) and National Insurance contributions for current and previous years if you're an employer.
items.changeNote: ‘2026 to 2027: Employer further guide to PAYE and National Insurance contributions’ has been updated with a new section ‘2.2.6 Relevant accretions’.

ai.summary: The guide explains how employers should handle PAYE and National Insurance contributions in less common situations.
ai.whoAffected: Employers, including SMEs and owner‑managed businesses, who need guidance on atypical PAYE/NIC matters
actions: Not stated in source

items.title: Valuation scales 2026
items.description: Find the 2026 valuation scales that the Valuation Office uses to value different parts of business properties depending on its floor level and how it's used.
items.changeNote: 'Offices modern standard with lift - London Docklands' has been replaced because the LAB accommodation use code has changed and 'Padel and tennis centres' has been added.

ai.summary: The 2026 valuation scales set relative values for parts of business properties based on floor level and use, with different scales for categories like central London offices versus other areas.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses that own, lease or occupy commercial property, including SMEs, owner‑managed firms and self‑employed property owners
actions: Identify each client’s property type and floor level to match the correct valuation scale
Determine if the property falls under multiple scales (e.g., central London office) and select the appropriate one
Apply the 2026 relative values when calculating business rates or tax liabilities
Update client records and advice notes with the new scale information

items.title: Choose the right software for Pillar 2 Top-up Taxes
items.description: Find out what commercial software is available to report Domestic Top-up Tax and Multinational Top-up Tax.
items.changeNote: The list of Pillar 2 commercial software suppliers has been updated with one amendment.

ai.summary: Domestic and Multinational Top‑up Taxes impose a 15% global minimum corporate tax on large groups for accounting periods starting on or after 31 Dec 2023. HMRC does not endorse any software; agents must ensure they have Pillar 2 access before selecting a solution.
ai.whoAffected: Large corporate groups and tax agents advising clients
ai.effectiveDate: Accounting periods beginning on or after 31 December 2023
actions: Confirm whether the client is required to report Pillar 2 Top‑up Taxes
Ensure you have Pillar 2 agent access in HMRC’s system
Evaluate commercial software options (HMRC does not recommend any)
If software issues arise, contact the software provider directly

items.title: More than £300 million paid out through Help to Save with thousands more savers set to benefit
items.description: Low income earners encouraged to open a Help to Save account in UK Savings Week.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: Help to Save, a government scheme giving low‑income earners a 50% bonus on savings up to £2,400, has paid out over £300 million. Eligibility expands in 2028 to all Universal Credit claimants and removes caring‑responsibility earnings test, adding about 1.5 million households. The scheme is now permanent.
ai.whoAffected: Low‑income earners, Universal Credit claimants, people with caring responsibilities, and their employers or advisors
actions: Notify eligible clients about the 2028 eligibility expansion and permanent status
Help clients check eligibility and open accounts via GOV.UK or the HMRC app
Advise clients to save £1‑£50 each month to maximise the 50% bonus
Track future eligibility changes and update client advice accordingly

items.title: Agent update: issue 147
items.description: Get guidance from HMRC if you're a tax agent or an adviser.
items.changeNote: General Betting Duty article has been updated to clarify the application of the new rate.

ai.summary: Agent updates provide guidance for tax agents and advisers; the next edition arrives in October 2026 and covers tax, borders, Making Tax Digital, HMRC services and engagement.
ai.whoAffected: Tax agents and advisers who support SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and the self‑employed
actions: Note the October 2026 release date for the next Agent Update
Sign up for email reminders to receive future editions
Review this month’s highlighted topics (tax, borders and trade, Making Tax Digital, HMRC services, agent engagement)
Apply the guidance in client advice where relevant

items.title: Inheritance Tax: jointly owned assets (IHT404)
items.description: Use the IHT404 with form IHT400 to give details of all UK assets the deceased owned jointly with another person.
items.changeNote: Schedule IHT404 has been updated to make it clearer where to enter spouse and charity exemption amounts.

ai.summary: Advisors must complete Schedule IHT404 with the IHT400 return to report any UK assets the deceased owned jointly with another person, using the updated guidance on spouse and charity exemptions.
ai.whoAffected: Personal representatives, accountants and advisors handling estates where the deceased held jointly‑owned UK assets
actions: Obtain Schedule IHT404 and the IHT400 estate return
Record all jointly‑owned UK assets on IHT404 as part of the IHT400 filing
Enter spouse and charity exemption amounts as clarified in the updated schedule
Submit the completed IHT404 with the IHT400 return to HMRC

items.title: HMRC email updates, videos and webinars for tax agents and advisers
items.description: Learn more about the support available to tax agents and advisers which will help you and your clients.
items.changeNote:
A new 'Multi-factor authorisation and what agents need to know' recorded webinar has been added.
The recorded webinar links for 'Overseas workday relief', 'Income from property for individual landlords — capital expenditure and revenue repairs' and 'Income from property for individual landlords — finance costs, travel expenses and the property income allowance' have been updated.
A link for a 'How to pay Vaping Products Duty and use Vaping Duty Stamps' live webinar has been added.

ai.summary: HMRC offers email updates and a range of live and recorded webinars for agents, covering Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, multi‑factor authentication, Pillar 2, and other reliefs. Agents must prepare clients, especially those with property or self‑employment income, for upcoming MTDT thresholds starting 6 April 2026.
ai.whoAffected: Tax agents and advisers, their SME/owner‑managed and self‑employed clients with income from property or self‑employment
actions: Subscribe to the HMRC help and support email service
Register for and attend relevant webinars (e.g., MTDT, MFA)
Check each client’s qualifying income against the MTDT thresholds and set up an Agent Services Account if needed
Advise clients to use HMRC‑recognised software and keep digital records throughout the year
legislationRefs: Making Tax Digital for Income Tax

items.title: Report Construction Industry Scheme (CIS) contractor monthly return errors if you've received a letter from HMRC
items.description: Tell HMRC about an error if they’ve sent you a letter about applying an incorrect rate to your subcontractor payments in tax year 2025 to 2026.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: HMRC letters indicate possible incorrect CIS rates for subcontractor payments in tax year 2025‑26. Contractors must report the error via the online CIS disclosure form, providing business details, UTR, letter reference and any underpaid tax. HMRC will review and respond within 28 working days.
ai.whoAffected: CIS contractors who have received an HMRC letter about an incorrect rate, including individuals, designated company members, trustees, estate representatives and authorised agents.
actions: Identify clients who received the HMRC letter about a CIS rate error
Use the HMRC CIS online service to complete the disclosure form
Gather required information: business name, UTR, letter reference (CFSS), and underpaid tax details
Submit the form and advise the client to await HMRC’s decision (usually within 28 working days)

items.title: Reduction in the cash Individual Savings Account (ISA) limit
items.description: This tax information and impact note is about changes to Individual Savings Account  (ISA) regulations to reduce the annual subscription limit of cash ISAs.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: The cash ISA annual subscription limit for people under 65 is reduced to £12,000 starting 6 April 2027, via changes to the Individual Savings Account Regulations 1998.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals aged under 65, including SME owners, partners and the self‑employed.
actions: Inform clients that the cash ISA limit will fall to £12,000 from 6 April 2027.
Review existing cash ISA contributions to ensure they do not exceed the new limit.
Discuss alternative tax‑efficient savings options if clients need to save more.
Update client records and advice notes to reflect the regulatory change.

items.title: Directors warned to verify identities with Companies House following first Insolvency Service prosecutions
items.description: Court action highlights legal duty on directors to complete identity verification
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: Directors must verify their identity with Companies House or face prosecution. The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 requires new directors to verify by 18 Nov 2025 and existing directors to do so within 12 months when filing their next confirmation statement. Recent fines show enforcement is active.
ai.whoAffected: Company directors (newly appointed and existing) and firms with unverified directors
actions: Check client director registers for verification status
Advise clients to complete identity verification online via Companies House or an authorised provider
Ensure the next confirmation statement is filed on time and includes verification
Monitor ongoing compliance and keep records to avoid prosecution
legislationRefs: Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023

items.title: Change your company accounting reference date (AA01)
items.description: Use this form to change an accounting reference date relating to either the current or immediately previous accounting period.
items.changeNote: Added wording for overseas companies with a UK establishment. They must send the paper form by post to the correct Companies House office.

ai.summary: Companies can change their accounting reference date using form AA01, must submit within the filing window, preferably online; overseas companies with UK establishments must post the paper form, and confirmation letters are no longer sent—check the new date online.
ai.whoAffected: Companies (including overseas companies with a UK establishment) that need to change their accounting reference date
actions: Advise the client to use the online service to submit the AA01 form for a quicker update
Ensure the submission is made within the period allowed for laying and delivering accounts for the current or immediately previous period
If the client is an overseas company with a UK establishment, instruct them to send the paper form by post to the correct Companies House office
Tell the client to search Companies House after filing to verify the new accounting reference date

items.title: Agents, Small and Mid-Sized Businesses Customer Survey 2025
items.description: This report describes the main findings from the department's 2025 Agents, Small and Mid-Sized Businesses Customer Survey.
items.changeNote: Data tables for the Agents, Small and Mid-Sized Businesses Customer Survey 2025 have now been added.

ai.summary: The 2025 Agents, Small and Mid‑Sized Businesses Customer Survey reports HMRC’s findings on agents, small and mid‑sized business experiences, compliance perceptions and reputation.
ai.whoAffected: Agents, small businesses and mid‑sized businesses

items.title: Individuals Customer Experience and Perceptions Survey 2025
items.description: This report describes the main findings from the department's 2025 Individuals Customer Experience and Perceptions Survey.
items.changeNote: Data tables for the Individuals Customer Experience and Perception Survey 2025 have now been added.

ai.summary: The 2025 Individuals Customer Experience and Perceptions Survey tracks overall customer experience and perceptions of HMRC, helping identify areas for service improvement for the individuals customer group.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals who are customers of HMRC

items.title: Verify your child for the childcare service
items.description: Use form CVF1 to verify your child for the childcare service.
items.changeNote: Information about the documents you need to send with form CVF1, to verify your child has been updated.

ai.summary: Use form CVF1 online to verify a child for childcare services, gathering a passport, birth or adoption certificate, and ensure a modern browser; submit the original document by post, not a photocopy.
ai.whoAffected: Parents or guardians needing to verify a child for the childcare service
actions: Gather the child’s passport, birth or adoption certificate before starting the online form
Complete the CVF1 form in one session (no saving) using an up‑to‑date browser
Submit the completed form and the original document by post (no photocopies)
Advise clients to keep a copy of the posted documents for their records

items.title: Compliance checks: penalties for CIS payments or returns connected to deliberate non-compliance — CC/FS96
items.description: This factsheet tells you about the penalties we may charge if we’ve issued a determination under either section 62A or 62B of the Finance Act 2004 for the Construction Industry Scheme (CIS).
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: This factsheet explains when HMRC may impose penalties for CIS payments or returns linked to deliberate non‑compliance, how penalties are calculated, notification methods, officer liability and your rights during the penalty process.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses and individuals making Construction Industry Scheme (CIS) payments or returns
actions: Check client CIS payments and returns for compliance with CIS rules
Maintain full records to support any HMRC calculations
Inform company officers of potential personal liability for CIS penalties
Promptly respond to any HMRC communication about possible penalties

items.title: Claim compensation for Childcare service issues
items.description: Check if you can get compensation if you’ve been unable to access Tax-Free Childcare or free childcare for working parents due to technical issues.
items.changeNote: 'What to do after you get compensation' section updated, as tax credit changes can no longer be reported to HMRC.

ai.summary: Parents who faced technical problems with the Childcare online service and missed Tax-Free Childcare top‑up or free childcare can claim compensation by completing an online form or writing to HMRC, providing proof of payments and account details. Universal Credit recipients must report any compensation to DWP.
ai.whoAffected: Parents who use Tax-Free Childcare or free childcare for working parents and have paid for childcare they should have received free
actions: Identify clients who experienced technical issues and paid for childcare
Help them complete the online form for Tax-Free Childcare top‑up and print/post it to HMRC
Assist clients to draft and send a letter with required details to the Childcare Service address for free childcare compensation
Advise Universal Credit claimants to report any compensation received to the Department for Work and Pensions

items.title: Hundreds of new officers to hunt down dirty money networks
items.description: Five hundred new officers to be recruited in a £500 million crackdown on money laundering, as part of the government's Anti-Money Laundering and Asset Recovery Strategy.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: The government will recruit 500 new officers, funded by £500 million, to target money‑laundering networks, seize criminal assets and strengthen AML supervision across police, NCA, CPS and professional services.
ai.whoAffected: SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed professionals, especially those in retail, hospitality and financial services that may face tighter AML supervision and scrutiny of high‑street premises
actions: Review client AML policies and ensure they meet the heightened supervision standards highlighted in the new strategy
Update record‑keeping and suspicious activity reporting procedures for clients in affected sectors
Advise high‑street retail and service clients on compliance to avoid being classified as ‘dodgy’ shops
Monitor guidance from the FCA, NCA and SFO for any new compliance requirements and relay updates to clients

items.title: The Finance Act 2026 (Scottish and Welsh Property Income Rates) (Appointed Day and Tax Year) Regulations 2026
items.description: The Regulations appoint 16th September 2026 as the day on which section 8 of, and Schedule 2 to, the Finance Act 2026 come into force. They also appoint the tax year 2027-28 as the first tax year in relation to which the amendments made by section 8 and Schedule 2 have effect. Those amendments accordingly have effect for the tax year 2027-28 and subsequent tax years.

items.title: Almost 7 million adults in the dark about their State Pension
items.description: HMRC is encouraging people to check their State Pension forecast using the HMRC app during Pension Awareness Week.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: HMRC urges all adults, especially 45‑54‑year‑olds, to use the free HMRC app during Pension Awareness Week (15‑18 Sept 2026) to check their State Pension forecast, view NI gaps and top‑up contributions, and consult the Tax Confident site for retirement tax advice.
ai.whoAffected: All UK adults, particularly 45‑54‑year‑olds, including employees, self‑employed and owners of SMEs
actions: Notify clients of Pension Awareness Week (15‑18 Sept 2026) and the need to check their State Pension forecast
Help clients download and access the free HMRC app to view their forecast and NI record
Identify any NI gaps and advise on eligible top‑up contributions
Refer clients to HMRC’s Tax Confident website for retirement tax guidance

items.title: The Finance Act 2009 (Publishing Details of Deliberate Tax Defaulters: Increase to Threshold) Order 2026
items.description: Section 94 of the Finance Act 2009 provides for the Commissioners for HM Revenue and Customs to publish information (including names) of persons who have been penalised for deliberate defaults where the tax lost exceeds £25,000.

items.title: Being a company director
items.description: Understanding your role as director of a limited company and your responsibilities to Companies House.
items.changeNote: Added a section 'Scam offering money to become a company director'. This section explains what to do if a recruiter offers you money to provide your identity details and be named as a director for an unknown company.

ai.summary: Directors must file annual accounts, confirmation statements and any changes with Companies House, ensure tax returns, and avoid conflicts of interest. New scam warns against paid director offers; victims should not share details, report fraud, and resign using TM01 if appointed.
ai.whoAffected: Current and prospective company directors, especially in SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed individuals who may be named as directors
actions: Advise clients to register for Companies House email reminders and file accounts and confirmation statements on time
Ensure directors understand their duties under the Companies Act 2006, including reporting changes and avoiding conflicts of interest
Warn clients about scams offering money to become a director; instruct them not to share personal details and to report any offer to Report Fraud online or 0300 123 2040
If a client has been appointed to a fraudulent company, guide them to resign via form TM01, keep records of the resignation and seek independent legal advice

items.title: PAYE draft forms: P45
items.description: Find approved final versions of form P45 for PAYE software developers.
items.changeNote: The Design specification for P45 (Online), P45 (Continuous), P45 (Continuous)(E), P45 (Laser continuous), P45 (Laser sheet), and P45 manual forms have been updated. Information about Tax credits and Universal Credit has been removed.

ai.summary: Draft P45 forms are provided for software developers creating substitute P45 forms.
ai.whoAffected: Software developers creating substitute P45 forms
actions: Identify if you are developing PAYE software that needs substitute P45 forms
Download the draft P45 forms from the GOV.UK source
Incorporate the draft designs into your software
Check that the generated forms meet HMRC specifications

items.title: Work out your qualifying income for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
items.description: Find out what counts as qualifying income from self-employment and property when using Making Tax Digital for Income Tax.
items.changeNote: The information about what you should do if all your self-employment and property income ceased before 6 April 2026 has been updated.

ai.summary: Qualifying income is the total pre‑expense turnover from self‑employment and property, taken from the previous year’s Self Assessment return. It determines whether a client must use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, unless all such income stopped before 6 April 2026.
ai.whoAffected: Self‑employed individuals and property owners (including sole traders and owners of jointly owned property) who may need to use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax.
actions: Check the client’s qualifying income from self‑employment and property using the previous tax year’s Self Assessment return.
If the income exceeds the relevant threshold, ensure the client signs up for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax and keeps digital records/quarterly updates.
If all self‑employment and property income ceased before 6 April 2026, advise the client to inform HMRC and file the final tax return showing income up to cessation.
If qualifying income falls below the threshold for three consecutive years, advise the client they may opt out of the service.

items.title: Check what to do if HMRC has signed you up for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
items.description: If you’ve been contacted by HMRC telling you we have signed you up, find out what steps you need to take next.
items.changeNote: Guidance has been updated to confirm HMRC will also check records against the 2025 to 2026 tax return if it's already been submitted. It's also been updated to make clear what you should do if all your income sources ceased before, on or from 6 April 2026.

ai.summary: HMRC may automatically enrol sole traders and landlords with income over £50,000 into Making Tax Digital for Income Tax. Clients must confirm HMRC’s records, adopt compatible software, create digital records, send quarterly updates and file the tax return.
ai.whoAffected: Sole traders and landlords with qualifying income over £50,000 in the 2024‑25 tax year, and any agents acting for them
actions: Check the client’s HMRC online account to confirm they have been signed up
Review and confirm the client’s income and expense details, adding new sources or noting ceased ones
Select and set up compatible MTDiT software to create digital records and send quarterly updates
Help the client catch up on any overdue quarterly updates and submit the 2026‑27 tax return

items.title: Simplified Process for Internal Market Movements (SPIMM): Category of goods guidance
items.description: Find out details about the different types of Category 1, Category 2 and Standard goods.
items.changeNote: Guidance has been amended to reflect the allowed use of I1 C&F and C21i EIDR NOP for Category 2 goods.

ai.summary: The Windsor Framework classifies GB‑to‑NI goods as Category 1, Category 2 or Standard, with Category 1 and 2 governed by Annex IX of the Withdrawal Agreement Joint Committee decision. Updated guidance now allows I1 C&F and C21i EIDR NOP for Category 2 goods.
ai.whoAffected: Businesses that move goods from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, including SMEs, owner‑managed firms and the self‑employed
actions: Determine whether each client’s goods are Category 1, Category 2 or Standard using the guidance
Review the specific requirements in Annex IX for Category 1 and Category 2 goods
Confirm that any Category 2 goods use the permitted I1 C&F and C21i EIDR NOP procedures

ai.summary: From 1 December 2026 objections to a limited company’s strike‑off must be filed via the Companies House “Make an objection” online service; email objections will no longer be accepted.
ai.whoAffected: Limited companies being struck off and anyone who needs to lodge an objection (e.g., directors, shareholders, creditors)
actions: Create a Companies House online account for the client
Gather the company name and registration number
Collect and prepare any supporting documents
Submit the objection through the Make an objection online service

items.title: Rates and thresholds for employers 2026 to 2027
items.description: Use these rates and thresholds when you operate your payroll or provide expenses and benefits to your employees.
items.changeNote: The advisory fuel rates for company cars have been updated.

ai.summary: From 6 April 2026 the personal allowance, PAYE tax bands, NI thresholds and rates, emergency tax codes, Class 1A/B rates and minimum wage rates change. Employers must apply the new figures when running payroll, calculating NI, benefits, termination awards and statutory pay.
ai.whoAffected: All UK employers, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed employers with staff, as well as directors
ai.effectiveDate: 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027 (specific rates from 1 April 2026 for minimum wage and from 5 April 2026 for SMP)
actions: Update payroll software with the new personal allowance, tax bands and NI thresholds/rates
Apply the updated emergency tax codes (1257L W1, M1, X) and Class 1A/B NI rates of 15%
Check that employee pay meets the new National Minimum Wage rates and adjust if needed
Use HMRC calculators to compute statutory maternity, paternity, adoption, parental bereavement and neonatal care payments at the new rates
legislationRefs: PAYE tax and Class 1 National Insurance contributions

items.title: Edition 6: Making Tax Digital for Income Tax — software developer newsletter
items.description: HMRC's newsletter for software developers for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: HMRC’s newsletter updates software developers on Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, covering recent changes, service performance and required developer actions, with the next edition due September 2026.
ai.whoAffected: Software developers creating MTD for Income Tax solutions
actions: Monitor the upcoming September 2026 edition
Review any service performance updates provided
Implement any developer actions outlined by HMRC
Stay informed of changes affecting MTD software

items.title: Scottish Income Tax outturn reconciliation for 2024-25
items.description: This explanatory note sets out how the 2024-25 Income Tax data published by HMRC and population data published by the ONS is used to update the Scottish Government’s funding.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: The 2024‑25 Scottish Income Tax outturn shows receipts below forecast, reducing self‑funding by £209 m and increasing the Block Grant Adjustment by £512 m, resulting in a net £720 m cut to Scottish Government funding for 2027‑28.
ai.whoAffected: Scottish Government (and indirectly Scottish public sector services)
actions: Update client briefing notes on the revised Scottish Government funding outlook
Monitor policy responses to the funding reduction
Advise clients on possible impacts to public services, grants or subsidies
Adjust financial forecasts for Scottish SMEs and self‑employed accordingly

items.title: Welsh Rates of Income Tax outturn reconciliation for 2024-25
items.description: This explanatory note sets out how the 2024-25 Income Tax data published by HMRC is used to update the Welsh Government’s funding.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: Actual 2024-25 Income Tax data shows Welsh Rates of Income Tax receipts above forecast, raising Welsh self‑funding by £129 m and cutting block‑grant adjustment by £17 m, netting a £146 m increase in overall funding for 2027‑28.
ai.whoAffected: Welsh Government and, indirectly, Welsh businesses and taxpayers
actions: Inform Welsh‑based SME clients that higher Welsh tax receipts may lead to increased public services funding
Monitor future Welsh Government budgets for spending changes linked to the £146 m funding boost
Advise clients on any potential tax compliance implications from revised Welsh Rates of Income Tax
Stay updated on further HMRC outturn releases affecting Welsh funding
legislationRefs: Fiscal Framework agreed between the UK and Welsh Governments in 2016

items.title: Construction Industry Scheme: CIS 340
items.description: Use this guidance and the examples included to help you if you are a contractor or subcontractor within the Construction Industry Scheme.
items.changeNote: Section 4.12 has been updated to explain that you need to provide your 13-character reference number when making payments to HMRC. A link to paying employers' PAYE has also been added.

ai.summary: Guidance outlines contractor and subcontractor roles under CIS and notes that payments to HMRC must include a 13‑character reference number per the updated Section 4.12, with a link to PAYE guidance added.
ai.whoAffected: Contractors and subcontractors operating under the Construction Industry Scheme
actions: Confirm each client’s 13‑character CIS reference number before making HMRC payments
Update payment templates to capture and transmit the reference number
Review the revised Section 4.12 for any additional compliance steps
Direct clients to the new PAYE link for employer payment information

items.title: Analysis of Ukrainian nationals entering employment in the UK
items.description: Counts of Ukrainian nationals in employment by age, gender and region in UK, England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
items.changeNote: Added Analysis of Ukrainian Nationals in employment in the UK, March 2022 to June 2026.

ai.summary: The release provides counts of Ukrainian nationals who registered for a National Insurance number on or after 4 March 2022 and were paid through PAYE, mainly those on humanitarian visa schemes. It is an ad‑hoc management information release, not official statistics.
ai.whoAffected: Ukrainian nationals entering UK employment via the Homes for Ukraine, Ukraine Family Scheme or Ukraine Extension Scheme, and UK employers hiring them
actions: Check that Ukrainian employees have a valid NINo before adding them to payroll
Process their earnings through PAYE as required
Inform clients that the data is management information, not official statistics
Monitor trends for workforce planning

items.title: Inheritance Tax on Pensions: Technical Note 2
items.description: This further technical note provides additional information to that provided in technical note 1 relating to Inheritance Tax on pensions announced at the Autumn Budget 2024.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: From 6 April 2027, unused pension funds and death benefits will count as estate assets for Inheritance Tax under the Finance Act 2026, with new information‑sharing, withholding and direct‑payment processes to be introduced.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals with pension savings, pension scheme trustees and estates of deceased persons
actions: Review client pension arrangements to identify unused funds and death benefits
Advise clients on potential IHT exposure from the new rules
Prepare for the information‑sharing and withholding notice requirements
Monitor forthcoming secondary legislation and HMRC guidance

items.title: Pension schemes newsletter 184 — August 2026
items.description: Newsletter 184, published by HMRC in August 2026 to update stakeholders on the latest news for pension schemes.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: HMRC's Pension Schemes Services newsletter 184 (August 2026) provides updates on the normal minimum pension age, non‑statutory clearances, disposal of non‑standard assets, a low‑earner pension payment update for scheme administrators, private pension statistics, pension savings statements and defined‑benefit scheme surplus payments to members.
ai.whoAffected: Pension scheme administrators and members of defined‑benefit pension schemes
actions: Review the normal minimum pension age rules for client schemes
Check clients' procedures for obtaining non‑statutory clearances
Assess how clients handle disposal of non‑standard assets
Update low‑earner pension payment processes for scheme administrators

items.title: Tell HMRC about any charges on special trusts (IHT100e)
items.description: Use this form to tell us that Inheritance Tax is due on assets that have stopped being held in special trusts.
items.changeNote: Information about what you must include if you're completing a declaration as a trustee has been added.

ai.summary: Use form IHT100e to notify HMRC that Inheritance Tax is due on a special trust, downloading it, opening it with Adobe Reader and completing it on‑screen; seek support if it won’t open.
ai.whoAffected: Trustees of special trusts where inheritance tax is due
actions: Download the IHT100e form and save it locally
Open the form with the latest free version of Adobe Reader
Complete the form on‑screen as required
If the form won’t open, contact online services support

items.title: Buildings and construction (VAT Notice 708)
items.description: How to work out the VAT on building work and materials if you're a contractor, subcontractor or developer.
items.changeNote: Electric vehicle charging points have been added to the list of zero-rated items for VAT in section '13.8.1 Dwellings'.

ai.summary: VAT notice 708 details when building work, materials, sales or leases are zero‑rated or reduced‑rated, the need for customer certificates, reverse charge rules, input‑tax blocks and self‑supply charges for contractors, subcontractors and developers.
ai.whoAffected: Contractors, subcontractors, developers, self‑builders and their customers (including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and the self‑employed).
actions: Check if the building work or material qualifies for zero‑rate or 5% reduced‑rate using the relevant sections of the notice
Obtain a signed certificate from the customer confirming the qualifying purpose before applying zero or reduced rates
Apply the VAT domestic reverse charge where the supplier and customer are UK‑VAT registered and the CIS reporting applies
Advise clients on input‑tax blocking rules for non‑building materials and on self‑supply obligations if the certificated use ceases or the building is disposed of
legislationRefs: VAT (Input Tax) Order 1992 (Statutory Instrument 1992/3222) articles 2 and 6
Value Added Tax Regulations 1995 (Statutory Instrument 1995/2518) Regulations 89 and 93
Value Added Tax (Self‑Supply of Construction Services) Order 1989 (Statutory Instrument 1989/472)

items.title: Find out about the Non-Statutory Clearance Service
items.description: How to use the Non-Statutory Clearance Service offered by HMRC for all customers and their advisers.
items.changeNote: The section 'When you can rely on information or advice given by HMRC' has been updated with information on when a clearance applies to you.

ai.summary: The Non‑Statutory Clearance Service lets clients request written HMRC advice on transactions where legislation is unclear, provided they have genuine uncertainty and have used all guidance. HMRC replies within 28 days (12 weeks for VAT), may request more info, and advice can be relied on if accurate and followed exactly.
ai.whoAffected: SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed individuals who need HMRC advice on transactions not covered by a statutory clearance
actions: Check whether the transaction is covered by a statutory clearance or another appropriate route before applying for non‑statutory clearance
Confirm the client has read all relevant guidance, cannot find the needed information and has a genuine uncertainty about the legislation
Prepare the application using the correct annex checklist (A‑E) and submit it to the specified email address, ensuring all information is accurate and complete

If HMRC requests additional information, provide it within 30 days and advise the client that the advice can be relied on only if the supplied details remain correct and the transaction is carried out as described
legislationRefs: Income Tax (Trading and Other Income) Act 2005

items.title: Apply for a certificate of residence or letter of confirmation
items.description: Use this form if you are a sole trader, company or organisation to get a certificate of residence or letter of confirmation so you do not pay tax twice on foreign income.
items.changeNote: A link to the new online form and information about who can apply and what happens after you apply has been added.

ai.summary: HMRC lets UK‑resident individuals, sole traders, companies and other entities apply online for a certificate of residence or a letter of confirmation to avoid double taxation, provided a double tax treaty exists. The application requires details of income, treaty, residency and supporting documents.
ai.whoAffected: Individuals, sole traders, partnerships, companies, trusts, charities, public bodies, pension schemes, collective investment schemes and other UK‑resident entities that may need to prove UK tax residence for double‑tax relief.
actions: Confirm the client is UK resident and a double taxation agreement exists with the relevant country.
Gather required information: treaty name, country, income type, period, residency details (days in UK, SRT justification, director/shareholder details for companies) and any supporting documents.
Submit the application online via HMRC’s service (or by post), ensuring any agent authorisation forms (APSS146A‑D) are included where needed.
For large businesses, request a pre‑order before the accounting period end if needed, and monitor HMRC’s response for the issued certificate or letter.
legislationRefs: chapter INTM120030 of the International manual
chapter INTM162000 of the International manual

items.title: How to avoid payslip fraud
items.description: Check that the tax and National Insurance shown on your payslip or deduction statement has been paid correctly if you’re an agency worker, temporary worker or contractor, or you work through an umbrella or payroll company.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: Payslip fraud occurs when tax, NI or CIS deductions shown on a payslip aren’t paid to HMRC, risking benefits, State Pension and tax bills. Regularly checking payslips, matching deductions to HMRC records and reporting mismatches protect workers, especially agency, temporary and CIS‑paid staff.
ai.whoAffected: Agency workers, temporary workers, contractors, umbrella‑company employees, self‑employed workers paid under the Construction Industry Scheme, CIS sub‑contractors, and anyone receiving payslips or deduction statements
actions: Advise clients to obtain a payslip for every pay period and verify personal, employer and tax‑code details
Instruct clients to compare tax and NI deductions on payslips with their Personal Tax Account, HMRC app, NI record or student loan account
Prompt clients to report any missing, false or mismatched payslips or CIS statements to HMRC promptly
For CIS sub‑contractors, ensure they include full invoice amounts and CIS deductions on their Self‑Assessment return and keep supporting evidence

items.title: Report an excepted estate for Inheritance Tax for deaths from 6 April 2011 to 31 December 2021 (IHT205)
items.description: Use the print and post form if the person died on or after 6 April 2011, and on or before 31 December 2021, and the estate is unlikely to pay Inheritance Tax.
items.changeNote: 'IHT206 notes to help you fill in form IHT205 (2011)' has been updated with new details on how to apply for an Inheritance Tax reference number.

ai.summary: Use the IHT205 print‑and‑post form for estates of people who died between 6 April 2011 and 31 December 2021 that are unlikely to pay Inheritance Tax, provided the deceased was a permanent resident of England, Wales or Northern Ireland.
ai.whoAffected: Executors or personal representatives of excepted estates (no IHT) for deaths between 6 April 2011 and 31 December 2021 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland
actions: Confirm the estate qualifies as an excepted estate (no IHT liability)
Download the IHT205 form and gather all required information before starting
Complete the form on‑screen using the latest free Adobe Reader
Print the completed form and post it to the address shown in the IHT206 notes; contact the online services helpdesk if you encounter issues

items.title: Apply for an agent services account if you're not based in the UK
items.description: Find out how to apply for approval to get an agent services account, if your agent business is based outside the UK.
items.changeNote: Guidance has been added for agents who do not need to register with a money laundering supervisory body in their country, including what evidence they need to provide. Confirmed the requirements for translated documents that are not in English.

ai.summary: Non‑UK‑based agents must get HMRC approval before creating an agent services account to access online services or use software for client communication. Applications are assessed against HMRC’s agent standards and require proof of trading address, AML registration (or exemption), tax registration and English translations where needed.
ai.whoAffected: Agents whose businesses are based outside the UK and need an HMRC agent services account to access online services or communicate with HMRC on behalf of clients
actions: Gather director’s details, business name, contact info and trading address (no PO Box)
Confirm AML supervisory registration or prepare a document explaining why it isn’t required, plus any membership details
Obtain proof of trading address, AML registration (if required) and tax registration, and provide English translations for non‑English documents
Create or use a Government Gateway ID and upload all required documents in one session to submit the application

items.title: Extra Statutory Concessions (VAT Notice 48)
items.description: This notice explains all of HMRC's Extra Statutory Concessions in force at the time of publication.
items.changeNote: Section 3.14 has been updated as Zero-rating of Certain Supplies of Free Zone Goods is no longer possible.

ai.summary: The notice lists HMRC’s Extra Statutory Concessions that are currently in force.
ai.whoAffected: Not stated in source
actions: Not stated in source

items.title: Claim a refund of Construction Industry Scheme deductions as a limited company
items.description: Get a refund of your Construction Industry Scheme (CIS) deductions if you're a subcontractor and you've had more taken than you need to pay in tax.
items.changeNote: Added information about how CIS refunds work, when you can claim, when evidence should be uploaded with a claim, how to use CIS deductions to pay another tax and what happens after a claim is submitted. Changed contact details to Employers: general enquiries.

ai.summary: Limited‑company subcontractors can claim a refund when CIS deductions exceed their tax liability. Claims can be made online for the last six years or by post for earlier years, and any surplus can be refunded or used to pay VAT or Corporation Tax.
ai.whoAffected: Limited company subcontractors (or agents representing them) who have had more CIS deductions taken than needed to cover their tax liabilities.
actions: Confirm the client is a limited‑company subcontractor with an over‑payment of CIS deductions
Collect required information: overpayment amount, company details, PAYE and Corporation Tax references, bank details and supporting statements
Submit the claim online (or by post for earlier years) using the client’s Corporation Tax/PAYE sign‑in or agent services account, attaching form R38 if paying an agent
Advise the client on options for any surplus – refund, or allocation to VAT or upcoming Corporation Tax – and monitor HMRC’s response within the stated timeframe

items.title: Sign up for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
items.description: If you're a sole trader or landlord, use the online service to sign up for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax.
items.changeNote: Information about what happens from September 2026 if you do not sign up to Making Tax Digital for Income Tax has been added.

ai.summary: Sole traders and landlords with self‑employment or property turnover over £50,000 must use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax from 6 April 2026. Sign up now or risk HMRC auto‑enrolling you from September 2026. Voluntary sign‑up is allowed, and penalties apply for late returns or payments.
ai.whoAffected: Sole traders and landlords whose combined self‑employment and property income exceeds £50,000, and their agents who sign clients up; also those below the threshold who may be exempt.
actions: Check each client’s self‑employment and property turnover against the £50,000 threshold.
Confirm the client is registered for Self Assessment and has filed a return in the past two years.
Ensure the client has compatible software and assist them to sign up via the online service (or advise voluntary sign‑up).
If the client has not signed up by September 2026, remind them to sign up or update their details before HMRC auto‑enrols them.

items.title: How to treat public service pensions remedy unauthorised payments
items.description: As a result of the public service pensions remedy (known as McCloud), members may have changes to, or new, unauthorised payments.
items.changeNote: The Secure Data Exchange Service has been renamed the Transfer files securely with HMRC service.

ai.summary: The public service pensions remedy can change members' unauthorised payments, affecting charges. Reductions may allow repayment and tax refunds; increases require new HMRC reporting. Scheme administrators must report changes, use the credit spreadsheet, and submit via the Transfer files securely with HMRC service.
ai.whoAffected: Members of public service pension schemes affected by the remedy, and their scheme administrators (including Chapter 1 administrators).
actions: Identify whether the member's unauthorised payment has been reduced or increased due to the remedy.
If reduced and an excess lump‑sum is repaid, advise the member to claim a refund of overpaid charges and assist with contacting HMRC.
If increased, ensure the member provides the required information to HMRC for the relevant tax years and report the new charge on the next event report.
Complete the credit spreadsheet and send it using the Transfer files securely with HMRC service to reclaim any overpaid scheme sanction charges.

items.title: Changes to how you sign in to the Find and update company information service
items.description: GOV.UK One Login will become the main sign-in option for the Find and update company information service.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: GOV.UK One Login will become the main sign‑in option for the Find and update company information service from late August 2026. Existing users can still use current details temporarily, but new users must have a One Login, and shared accounts must be split into individual logins.
ai.whoAffected: All users of the Find and update company information service, including SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed who access Companies House services, especially those using shared company accounts
actions: Advise clients to create their own GOV.UK One Login linked to an individual email and phone
Review any shared Companies House accounts and plan separate individual accounts
Notify clients of the upcoming sign‑in change and the need for MFA setup
Ensure clients set up an authenticator app or SMS for multi‑factor authentication

items.title: Agent Update: issue 146
items.description: Get guidance from HMRC if you're a tax agent or an adviser
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: Agent Updates provide guidance for tax agents and advisers; the next edition is due September 2026 and covers tax, borders and trade, Making Tax Digital, HMRC services and agent engagement. Sign up for email alerts.
ai.whoAffected: Tax agents and advisers
actions: Review the current Agent Update for relevant guidance
Note that the next edition will be published in September 2026
Sign up for email reminders to receive future editions
Monitor the highlighted topics (tax, borders and trade, Making Tax Digital, HMRC services, agent engagement)

items.title: HMRC email updates, videos and webinars for employing people
items.description: Learn more about getting started as an employer or running a small business including registration, payroll, tax returns, tax bills and payments.
items.changeNote: Live webinars for 'Employees with more than one workplace', 'Employee travel', 'Phones, internet and homeworking' and 'Trivial benefits' have been added. The webinar links for 'Company cars, vans and fuel' and 'Labour supply chain due diligence for local authorities' have been updated.

ai.summary: HMRC offers email updates, videos and live/recorded webinars covering employer registration, payroll, tax codes, benefits, statutory pay and other obligations, helping new and existing employers manage taxes, reporting and compliance.
ai.whoAffected: Employers and small‑business owners, including owner‑managed businesses and self‑employed people who employ staff
actions: Subscribe to the HMRC help and support email service for updates
Register clients for relevant live webinars (e.g., employer filing obligations, payroll, trivial benefits)
Direct clients to the video collections for new‑employer guidance, tax codes and running a small business
Advise clients to use their HMRC business tax account to add and manage taxes such as PAYE, Corporation Tax, Self Assessment and VAT

items.title: Employer Bulletin: August 2026
items.description: A bi-monthly magazine for employers and agents that gives up-to-date information on payroll topics.
items.changeNote: Added translation

ai.summary: The August 2026 Employer Bulletin outlines guidance on making PAYE Settlement Agreement payments, the phased roll‑out of mandatory benefits‑in‑kind payrolling, consultations on lower‑value tax debts and aligning NI recovery limits with Income Tax, plus help for parent or carer employees to claim Child Benefit.
ai.whoAffected: Employers, payroll agents and employees who are parents or carers
actions: Advise clients to ensure their PAYE Settlement Agreement payment is made as required
Prepare clients for the upcoming mandatory payrolling of benefits in kind by reviewing current processes
Monitor the government consultations on low‑value tax debts and NI recovery time limits and inform clients of any changes
Assist client employees who are parents or carers in claiming their entitled Child Benefit

items.title: Order certified documents and certificates from Companies House
items.description: How to order certified copies of certificates and documents held on the Companies House register.
items.changeNote: The message about being unable to process requests for company certificates until further notice has been removed. The issue has been resolved.

ai.summary: Companies House lets you order certified company certificates or document copies via its online service or phone, with standard (£22) or express (£65) dispatch. You can add extra facts, but not PSC or share details. Legalisation is possible through the FCDO for Hague Convention countries.
ai.whoAffected: SMEs, owner‑managed companies and their advisers who need certified copies or certificates from Companies House
actions: Advise clients to order certificates or copies using the Find and update service or call 0303 1234 500
Recommend choosing standard or express dispatch, noting costs and timelines, and checking for postal delays
Ensure clients request any additional certified facts needed, remembering restrictions on PSC, shareholders and capital statements
If a document is needed abroad, guide clients to legalise it through the FCDO, confirming it has a British official’s original signature

items.title: Extend Child Benefit for your teen before 31 August
items.description: Parents have until 31 August to extend Child Benefit for their 16 to 19-year-olds who are continuing in non-advanced approved education or training.
items.changeNote: First published.

ai.summary: Parents must extend Child Benefit for 16‑19‑year‑olds in non‑advanced education by 31 August 2026 or payments stop; can be done online, by post or phone; check HICBC liability if income exceeds £60,000.
ai.whoAffected: Parents of 16‑ to 19‑year‑old children who are continuing in non‑advanced approved education or training, including self‑employed parents
actions: Identify clients with 16‑19‑year‑old children in approved education and confirm they have extended their claim
Advise clients to extend the claim via the HMRC app or GOV.UK before the 31 August deadline
If digital access is unavailable, guide clients to use the post or phone method detailed in their HMRC letter
Remind clients with an individual adjusted net income over £60,000 to assess any High Income Child Benefit Charge using the online calculator

items.title: Apply for an exemption from Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
items.description: Find out how to apply for an exemption from Making Tax Digital for Income Tax.
items.changeNote: Information about 'When to apply' for an exemption if you need to use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax from 6 April 2027 has been updated.

ai.summary: Clients may be exempt from Making Tax Digital for Income Tax if they are digitally excluded or meet other criteria; they must apply to HMRC with personal details and reasons, and continue filing Self Assessment as normal.
ai.whoAffected: Self Assessment taxpayers, including self‑employed individuals and owners of SMEs who may need to use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
actions: Check whether the client is automatically exempt or needs to apply for an exemption
Collect the client’s NI number, address and a written explanation (including digital‑exclusion evidence if relevant)
Submit the application by calling or writing to HMRC using the correct subject line for the exemption type
If the application is refused, advise the client on the 30‑day appeal process and maintain normal Self Assessment record‑keeping

items.title: HMRC email updates, videos and webinars if you’re self-employed
items.description: Learn more about your responsibilities if you’re running a small business including registration, tax returns, record keeping, tax bills and payments.
items.changeNote:

ai.summary: HMRC offers email updates and a range of live and recorded webinars covering tax basics, record keeping, Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, and Self Assessment, plus YouTube video guides for self‑employed and small business owners.
ai.whoAffected: Self‑employed individuals, sole traders, partnerships, landlords and joint property owners, and small business owners seeking guidance on tax obligations
actions: Subscribe clients to the HMRC help and support email service
Recommend and register clients for relevant live webinars (e.g., tax basics, record keeping, MTD, Self Assessment) and advise joining 5 minutes early
Provide links to recorded webinars and YouTube video collections for self‑assessment, MTD and property income guidance
Guide clients on using the resources to understand registration, record keeping, software choices and filing deadlines

items.title: HMRC tools and calculators
items.description: Find and use tools and calculators that will help you work out your tax.
items.changeNote: A 'Deadlines' section has been added to help you find out the filing and payment deadlines for your taxes, and add them to your calendar.

ai.summary: HMRC provides an extensive suite of online tools and calculators covering duties, allowances, taxes, benefits and compliance checks, including a new Deadlines tool to help clients track filing and payment dates, useful for SMEs, owner‑managed firms and the self‑employed.
ai.whoAffected: SMEs, owner‑managed businesses, self‑employed individuals, partnerships, limited companies, directors, employees, trustees and anyone needing to calculate tax, duties or compliance obligations
actions: Identify which HMRC tools are relevant to each client’s situation and bookmark them
Use the new Deadlines tool to add filing and payment dates to the practice’s calendar
Guide clients to specific calculators (e.g., Small Producer Relief, Capital Allowances, Self‑Assessment, VAT) to improve accuracy
Record tool usage and outcomes for client records and future reference

items.title: HMRC Trusts and Estates newsletters
items.description: Newsletters published by HMRC, giving updates and guidance on Inheritance Tax and trusts.
items.changeNote: The HMRC Trusts and Estates Newsletter for August 2026 has been added.

ai.summary: HMRC newsletters provide trusts and estates practitioners with the latest non‑binding news and views as of their publication date, with older issues available via the National Archives.
ai.whoAffected: trusts and estates practitioners (including advisers to SMEs, owner‑managed businesses and the self‑employed)
actions: Subscribe to the HMRC Trusts and Estates newsletters
Review each issue for updates relevant to client trusts or estates
Remember the content is not legally binding and confirm against current legislation
Access older newsletters through the National Archives when needed

items.title: Check your tax filing and payment deadlines
items.description: Use this tool to find out your tax deadlines and add them to your calendar.
items.changeNote: Added translation

ai.summary: The HMRC tool lets contractors, employers, self‑assessment and VAT users enter their details to get personalised tax filing and payment deadlines, which can be printed or added to digital calendars.
ai.whoAffected: Contractors (CIS), employers (PAYE), self‑assessment taxpayers and VAT‑registered businesses, including SMEs and the self‑employed
actions: Collect each client’s accounting period dates, tax payment method and filing method (online or post)
Enter the information into the HMRC deadline tool to generate specific dates
Print the deadline list or add it to the client’s calendar (use Safari for Apple Calendar on iPhone/iPad)
Remind clients to file returns and pay taxes by the generated deadlines

items.title: Consultation on Simplifying Treaty Relief from Withholding Tax on Interest Paid Overseas
items.description: We welcome views on simplification of the process to obtain treaty relief in relation to withholding tax obligations when making payments of interest overseas.
items.changeNote: Updated to include information for a virtual roundtable event.

ai.summary: HMRC is consulting on simplifying the process for obtaining treaty relief from withholding tax on overseas interest payments, aiming to ease administration while preventing avoidance. Stakeholders are invited to a virtual roundtable on 3 Sept 2026 and to submit written views.
ai.whoAffected: Taxpayers making interest payments overseas, especially those involved in cross‑border financing and using existing treaty relief processes (e.g., Double Taxation Treaty Passport, Directions to make payments at the treaty rate).
actions: Identify clients who make overseas interest payments and may need treaty relief
Review their current treaty relief processes (Double Taxation Treaty Passport, Directions, claims)
Register for the virtual roundtable by emailing the address before 26 Aug 2026 (max 2 participants per firm)
Prepare and submit written responses to the consultation
